actions.justification: MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: blood cultures must be obtained BEFORE administering antibiotics to identify causative organism. This is especially critical in a neutropenic patient with ANC 200 where bacteremia is highly likely.

MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: serum lactate must be measured within 1 hour to assess tissue perfusion and guide resuscitation. Elevated lactate (>=4 mmol/L) would trigger 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus.

MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics must be administered within 1 hour of sepsis recognition, immediately after blood cultures are obtained. Febrile neutropenia with sepsis requires anti-pseudomonal coverage (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime).
Patient has hypotension (BP 100/60, MAP 73) meeting criteria for 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus per SSC Hour-1 Bundle guidelines. Fluid resuscitation should begin immediately.
Evaluate for end-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, coagulation, neurologic) to determine sepsis severity and guide further management. ANC 200 with fever indicates high-risk febrile neutropenia.
Identify potential infection source (central line, mucositis, pulmonary, GI) in this post-chemotherapy neutropenic patient to guide targeted antimicrobial therapy and source control.

Serial vital sign monitoring is essential to evaluate hemodynamic response to the 30mL/kg crystalloid bolus already given. Patient remains tachycardic (HR 112) with borderline BP 100/60 - need to reassess MAP and determine if vasopressor support is required to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg per SSC guidelines.

CBC is critical in this neutropenic patient (ANC 200, post-chemotherapy day 10) to confirm current blood counts, assess for thrombocytopenia or anemia complicating resuscitation, and guide management of febrile neutropenia per oncologic sepsis protocols.

Basic metabolic panel assesses renal function (creatinine/BUN), electrolytes, and glucose — critical for evaluating organ dysfunction in sepsis, guiding fluid management, and identifying acute kidney injury which is a common sepsis complication.

Initial lactate was 2.8 mmol/L (>2 mmol/L), per SSC guidelines serial lactate measurements are recommended to guide resuscitation and assess response to treatment. At 45 minutes post-arrival, a repeat lactate is indicated.

Patient has HR 112, BP 100/60, MAP 73 with recent fluid administration. Reassessing perfusion status (mental status, urine output, skin perfusion) is essential to determine adequacy of resuscitation and whether vasopressors are needed.

MAP is borderline at 73 mmHg (just above 65 threshold) in a septic patient with elevated lactate and tachycardia. Given the patient's hemodynamic instability and neutropenic sepsis, early vasopressor readiness is warranted. If MAP drops below 65 after fluid bolus or perfusion remains inadequate, norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor per SSC guidelines.
Patient with AML on chemotherapy with sepsis is at high risk for DIC. Coagulation studies (PT/INR/aPTT/fibrinogen) are indicated to assess for coagulopathy and guide management.

Procalcitonin provides a baseline biomarker for bacterial infection severity and can guide antibiotic stewardship decisions and serial monitoring of treatment response in this neutropenic febrile patient.
Chest X-ray is indicated to evaluate for pulmonary source of infection (pneumonia, fungal infiltrates) in this immunocompromised patient with tachypnea (RR 22) and no identified infection source.

Patient has persistent hypotension (MAP 73, borderline) with lactate 2.8 and is on vasopressors; additional crystalloid bolus supports ongoing resuscitation per SSC guidelines for fluid responsiveness assessment.
Continuous arterial pressure monitoring is indicated given hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors, allowing real-time MAP trending and frequent lab sampling without repeated venipuncture.
Central venous access is needed for reliable vasopressor administration (norepinephrine), CVP monitoring, and potential escalation to additional vasoactive agents in this septic shock patient.

Patient remains hemodynamically compromised (MAP 73, HR 112, BP 100/60) and is already on norepinephrine. Per SSC guidelines, vasopressin can be added as a second vasopressor to achieve MAP ≥65 mmHg or to reduce norepinephrine dose. This is the only remaining available action and is clinically appropriate for refractory septic shock in this neutropenic AML patient.

Patient has septic shock with persistent hypotension (MAP 73 on vasopressors), tachycardia, elevated lactate 2.8, and is neutropenic (ANC 200) post-chemotherapy — ICU-level care is mandatory for close monitoring and ongoing resuscitation.
